title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: With regard to military matters, Napoleon immediately upon entering Moscow gave General Sebastiani strict orders to monitor the Russian army's movements, sent army corps along the various roads, and instructed Murat to find Kutuzov. Then he gave careful directions about the fortification of the Kremlin and drew up a brilliant plan for a future campaign covering the entire map of Russia.

With regard to diplomatic questions, Napoleon summoned Captain Yakovlev—who had been robbed, was dressed in rags, and had no idea how to get out of Moscow—and explained his entire policy and his magnanimity in great detail. Having written a letter to Emperor Alexander in which he felt duty-bound to inform his Friend and Brother that Rostopchin, the governor of Moscow, had badly mismanaged things in Moscow, he dispatched Yakovlev to Petersburg.
Having similarly explained his views and his magnanimity to Tutolmin, he sent that old man off to Petersburg to negotiate as well.
With regard to legal matters, immediately after the fires, he ordered that the arsonists be found and executed. And the scoundrel Rostopchin was punished by an order to burn down his houses.
With regard to administrative matters, Moscow was granted a constitution. A municipal government was established and the following announcement issued:

Your misfortunes are terrible, but His Majesty the Emperor and King wishes to end them. Harsh examples have shown you how he punishes disobedience and crime. Strict measures have been taken to restore order and public safety. A fatherly administration, chosen from among yourselves, will form your municipality or city government. It will care for you, your needs, and your welfare. Its members will be marked by a red ribbon worn across the shoulder, and the mayor will also wear a white belt. But when not on duty, they will wear only a red ribbon on the left arm.

The city police has been restored on its former basis, and its activity has already improved public order. The government has appointed two commissaries general, or police chiefs, and twenty commissaries or captains of wards have been appointed to the different wards of the city. You will know them by the white ribbon on their left arm. Several churches of various denominations are open, and services continue without interference. Your fellow citizens are returning daily, and orders have been given that they shall find in them the help and protection due to their misfortunes. These are the government's measures to restore order and ease your condition. But to achieve this, you must add your own efforts: forget, if possible, the misfortunes you've suffered; should entertain the hope of a less cruel fate; be certain that inevitable, shameful death awaits anyone who threatens your persons or your remaining property; and you should not doubt that these will be safeguarded, since such is the will of the greatest and most just of monarchs. Soldiers and citizens, whatever your nation—restore public trust, the foundation of a state's welfare. Live as brothers, give each other aid and protection, unite to defeat the intentions of the evil-minded, obey the military and civil authorities, and your tears will soon dry!

With regard to supplies for the army, Napoleon decreed that all troops should take turns entering Moscow à la maraude * to obtain provisions for themselves, so that the army might have its future provided for.
With regard to religion, Napoleon ordered the priests brought back and services resumed in the churches.
With regard to commerce and to provisioning the army, the following was posted everywhere:

You, peaceful citizens of Moscow, artisans and workers driven from the city by misfortune, and you scattered farmers still kept out in the fields by groundless fear—listen! Peace is returning to this capital and order is being restored. Your countrymen are emerging boldly from hiding, finding they are treated with respect. Any violence to them or their property is promptly punished. His Majesty the Emperor and King protects them and considers none of you his enemy except those who disobey his orders. He wishes to end your suffering and return you to your homes and families. Respond, therefore, to his benevolent intentions and come to us without fear. Citizens, return confidently to your dwellings! You will soon find ways to meet your needs. Craftsmen and industrious artisans, return to your trades, your homes, your shops, where guards await to protect you! You will receive proper pay for your work. And lastly you too, peasants, come from the forests where you are hiding in terror, return to your huts without fear, knowing you will find protection! Markets have been set up in the city where peasants can bring their surplus supplies and the products of the soil. The government has taken the following steps to ensure freedom of sale for them: (1) From today, peasants, husbandmen, and those living in the neighborhood of Moscow may safely bring supplies of all kinds to two designated markets—one on Mokhovaya Street and the other at the Provision Market. (2) Goods will be purchased at prices agreed between buyer and seller, and if a seller cannot get a fair price, he may freely take his goods back to his village, and no one may hinder him under any pretense. (3) Sundays and Wednesdays are the main market days, with sufficient troops stationed along the highways on Tuesdays and Saturdays at such distances from the town as to protect the carts. (4) Similar measures will be taken that peasants with their carts and horses may meet with no hindrance on their return journey. (5) Steps will be taken immediately to restore normal trade.

Citizens and villagers, workers and artisans of all nations—you are called to carry out the fatherly intentions of His Majesty the Emperor and King and to work with him for the common good! Place your respect and confidence at his feet and join us without delay!

To raise the spirits of both troops and civilians, reviews were constantly held and rewards distributed. The Emperor rode through the streets to comfort the residents and, despite his preoccupation with state affairs, personally attended the theaters he had ordered to be set up.

In regard to philanthropy, the greatest virtue of crowned heads, Napoleon did everything in his power. He had the words Maison de ma Mère (House of My Mother) inscribed on charitable institutions, blending tender filial devotion with a monarch's majestic generosity. He visited the Foundling Hospital and, allowing the orphans he had saved to kiss his white hands, conversed graciously with Tutolmin. Then, as Thiers eloquently recounts, he ordered his soldiers to be paid in forged Russian currency he had prepared: "Raising the use of these means by an act worthy of himself and of the French army, he let relief be distributed to those who had been burned out. But as food was too precious to give to foreigners—most of whom were enemies—Napoleon preferred to supply them with money to buy food from outside, and had paper rubles distributed to them."
With reference to army discipline, orders were continually issued imposing severe punishment for the nonperformance of military duties and to suppress looting.
